items.text: If the other side violates protection rules first, its cultural property may be made the object of reprisals.
Failure by the State where cultural property is located to adopt the Convention’s safeguard measures does not relieve another country of its obligation to respect such cultural property.
The obligations may be waived only when imperatively required by military necessity; waiver cannot be claimed merely on the ground of ordinary military convenience.
If cultural property was not directly targeted, there is no need to assess required precautions or the proportionality of incidental damage.
Limited military-necessity exceptions to cultural-property protection may exist where the applicable law provides for them and its strict conditions are satisfied.
Confirmed damage to cultural property is sufficient to establish that a particular individual committed a war crime, without any additional evidence.
When cultural-property status and other relevant conditions are the same, protection obligations should not change because of the country to which the property belongs.
The loss of a country's important cultural property can also be a loss to the cultural heritage of all humanity.
A political judgment about a country's government should not, by itself, justify lowering protection standards for that country's cultural property.
Lower protection standards may be applied to cultural property solely because it belongs to a politically hostile country.
Even when a cultural tradition differs from one familiar to the evaluator, its important cultural property should be protected under the same relevant rules.
The occurrence of armed conflict does not, by itself, automatically cancel obligations to respect cultural property.
